title: Chapter 3: Cause Unseen
blurb: Ravi blames the thing that chews, and a stranger knows his surname.

blocks.text: I had my ear against riser 2's cupboard on the fourth-floor landing, listening to something small chew, when the tenants' association came into the lobby with a list of every key that had gone missing from flats 2B and 3A.

I could hear Mrs Quarry from four floors up. I could hear the teeth better. They were a foot above the top of the cupboard door, where the fourth floor's ceiling was and the fifth floor wasn't supposed to be, and they were working at something with the patience of a woman shelling peas.
"I know," I told the casing, and coughed. It came up like a shovel going into wet gravel. "I know you're in there. I can't do a thing about you yet. The book won't have me."

Four nights running I'd gone down to the office and tried to sign for some other job on floor 5, anything I could finish, and every time the nib had skated across the TAKEN BY line as if the paper had been waxed. One order at grade nought. Walter had told me. I'd needed to watch the pen do it anyway.
"Mr Anand!" Mrs Quarry, from the lobby. "We are convened!"

The association was Mrs Quarry from 3A, who chaired it, and Gil Ferrabee from 2B, who was the rest of it. They stood by the post table with a sheet of lined paper between them like a summons. Dusty was asleep under the table. Mrs Wrobel sat on the bottom stair in her cardigan, not part of the association, she'd have told you, just a woman waiting for her post at seven in the evening.
"Every hook," Mrs Quarry said. "Every single hook. Spare front door. Window locks. The meter cupboard. Gil's bicycle."
"The bike's still there," said Gil. "It's the lock key. I'm locked to a drainpipe."
"My late mother's jewellery box, which is empty, but that is not the point."
"They took the ring and left the fob," said Gil. "Who does that, Ravi?"
I coughed into my elbow, which was a mistake, because Mrs Quarry took a step back and wrote something on the list.
"We're not saying anything," she said. "We're only noting that one person in this building has keys to everything."

"I've got keys to the boiler room and the bins," I said. "And the lift." All true, and from her face the worst thing I could have said. So I asked about the hooks. "Where do your keys hang? Which wall?"
"By the kitchen door."
"Which side of it?"
She had to think. "The side with the boxing in. The pipe box."
"Same," said Gil.

Riser 2's casing. It came down through every flat on that side of the building, boxed in behind board and painted whatever colour the tenant fancied, and in both their kitchens someone sixty years ago had screwed a row of brass hooks into it because it was the handiest thing by the door. I'd have done the same. I stood in the lobby and pictured the casing going up through 2B and 3A and past 4C's landing to the ceiling line, and the teeth sitting just above it, and I couldn't make the last part work. Nothing I'd heard had come lower than the top of the fourth floor. The keys had gone from two and three floors further down.
"Give me a couple of nights," I said. "I want to see where they're going."
"Where they're *going*?" said Mrs Quarry.
"Where they're being taken. By whoever."
"Wear them," said Mrs Wrobel from the stairs. She lifted a string out of the neck of her cardigan with one Yale on it and let it drop back. "Round the neck. Day and night. Like me."
"Thank you, Nessa," said Mrs Quarry, in the voice of a chair accepting a point of order, and wrote that down too.

I hadn't spoken to Mrs Wrobel properly since the soup. That night I'd shut the cupboard, like she told me, and then I'd told her which floor, because she'd asked twice and I didn't know how to lie to a woman holding my supper. I'd said five. She had nodded once, as if I'd told her the time, taken her pan in and shut her door. Every night since, she'd said good evening and nothing else. I'd decided she thought I was having her on and wasn't going to dignify it, and that it was kinder all round to let her.
She watched me go down to the basement. She didn't say good evening.
At eleven I took the lift up. Dusty walked me as far as the service corridor, looked at the open cage, and lay down across the threshold with his chin on his paws.
"Coming?"
He sighed through his nose and stayed where he was. He hadn't been up with me since the night he talked. I'd put it down to his hips, or his opinion of me, and I hadn't liked to ask which.

Floor 5 was how I'd left it: the brown lino, the dado rail, the bulbs in their bowls, and the ones near the stair door flickering like they were trying to remember something. I talked to them on the way past.
Riser 2's cupboard smelled of wet iron. I opened it and put the torch on the joints.

They'd been weeping when I took the order. Now they'd been bitten. Every collar down the run had fresh marks in the lead caulking, little crescents, bright as new pennies where the teeth had gone through the grey, and on the two worst joints they'd gone into the iron itself. I ran my thumb over one. Clean edges, a day old at most. The water came out worst exactly where the bites were deepest. A couple of them had a fine white fluff in the bottom, which I took for old lagging they'd dragged in, and under the iron there was a smell like a punnet of mushrooms left in a bag. I put that down to the unnumbered door along the corridor, which smelled the same every night and which I still hadn't opened.
At the foot of the chase, where the pipe went down through the floor, there was a nest.

It was the size of a mixing bowl and built out of keys. Yales, mortice keys, little padlock keys, bent and plaited together through their bows the way you'd weave a basket, and wedged in round the pipe where it went into the slab. Some were chewed to stubs. Some were whole. Hooked on near the rim by its ring was a brass fish about two inches long, and I knew it, because I'd seen it hanging by Mrs Quarry's kitchen door the day I bled her radiator.

Something in the nest moved. I got the torch on it in time to see an eye like a drop of oil and a body the size and colour of an old Yale, and then it was down among the keys, and there was a small sound like a key going into a lock and turning.

"Evening," I said. My voice was perfectly steady. It just didn't stop. "Don't get up. I'm only looking. That's a lot of keys you've got. That's Mrs Quarry's fish, that is. She'll want that back. And you've been at my joints as well, haven't you. You have. I can see your teeth in them."
I sat back on my heels and coughed, and nothing answered.

So there it was. Small things that ate keys, nesting where the pipe went through, and their bites all down the run. The joints weren't failing on their own. Something was eating them, and I'd been carrying a cough for five days for a pest's supper.
Dusty came down to the office with me, which he never did, and lay across the doorway as if somebody might try to leave.
The Works Book was open at floor 5. I sat in front of it and coughed and didn't pick up the pen.
"Right," I said to the dog. "Here's what I've got."
He opened one eye.
"I can write the cause. Key-eaters. Whatever they're really called, that's what they do. I write it, I fit the joints from Ropewalk Lane, I sign it off at the fault, and the cough goes. Yes?"
Nothing.
"And tomorrow night they eat the new ones."
He sighed, which I took as agreement.

I'd bought the joints the morning after I took the order. They were in a box under the desk with the receipt still in it. I hadn't fitted them because I hadn't known what was wrong, and I don't put my name to a cause I haven't seen. That's an old rule of mine. It's cost me before.
"So I don't want to just fix it," I said. "Not yet. I want them to stop."

Every order had a CAUSE line. A book that only wanted a pipe mended wouldn't care why it broke. On every site I'd ever worked, the cause was what everybody fought over, because whoever caused the damage paid for it. You sent the bill to the electrician who'd put his drill through your pipe. Back-charge, we called it.
"'Till you sign it off at the fault, or,'" I said. "That's what he told me. Your Walter. Or what?"
Dusty looked at the wall.
"And it's triplicate." I lifted the carbon with one finger. "One copy stays in the book. One I sign at the fault. Every triplicate docket I ever had, the third one went to whoever was being charged."
He put his head on his paws and sighed again, the way he does when the bins go out late, and I couldn't have told you whether it meant yes or I'd rather you didn't.
I didn't know what the book did if I got a cause wrong. Walter hadn't said, and I couldn't ask him in a basement. But I'd seen the teeth. I'd had my thumb in them.
I wrote it. There was no line for whoever I was charging, so I put that underneath, small, the way you'd write an address on the back of an envelope.

``` WO-5-002 FLOOR 5. TIER 1. FAULT: RISER 2, JOINTS FAILING. LEAK. PEST PASSAGE TO FLOORS 1-4. CAUSE: Key-eaters, nesting at foot of riser 2 chase. Gnawing the joints. GRADE REQUIRED: 1. SYMPTOM: WET CHILL. WATERY COUGH. STATUS: OPEN. TAKEN BY: R. Anand To: the key-eaters, riser 2, floor 5. ```
The ink took. It didn't skate. I tore the slip off along its perforations and it came away clean, my own writing on it in carbon blue.
Dusty stayed at the lift gate again. I went up on my own with the slip in my top pocket.
Something in the nest was awake. I could hear the turning sound, like somebody trying key after key in a door that wasn't theirs.
I knelt, my chest full of cold water.

"Sorry," I said. "I'm sorry about this. You've made yourselves a home and I've come round with a bill for it, and I know how that feels from the other end." I held the slip up so whatever it was could see it, which was daft. "I won't touch anything. Not the fish, not any of it. I'll leave it all exactly the way I found it. You've got my word."
I folded the slip once, longways, slid it between two Yales at the rim into the mouth of the nest with two fingers, and took my fingers out again.

For a second, nothing. Then the cold went out of my chest the way bathwater goes when you pull the plug, all at once and from underneath, and I breathed in right to the bottom of my lungs for the first time in five days and didn't cough.
From inside the nest came a cough.
It was tiny, and wet. It was my cough, the exact one, made small enough to fit something the size of a Yale, and it caught and started again the way mine had. Then a second one joined it.
I sat back on the lino.
"Oh," I said. "Oh, no. That's what that does."
The brass fish was by my thumb. Mrs Quarry could have had it back by breakfast, and nobody but me would have known.
I'd said exactly the way I found it. I took my hand back, shut the cupboard door gently on the coughing, and went down without the fish.
In the office the entry had moved on without me. My handwriting was still there. The copperplate had changed one word on the floor's page, as calmly as if it had always been that way.
``` WO-5-002  RISER 2, JOINTS FAILING    TRANSFERRED
CARETAKER: R. ANAND GRADE: 0 CREDITS: 3 HOLDING: 0 CERTIFIED: NONE ```
Still red. Of course it was. I hadn't fixed a single joint; I'd handed the job to somebody smaller. Three credits, and not one for tonight. I wouldn't have paid me either.
Holding nought, though. The slot was free.

I turned to the door to 5-1, swollen in its frame, the job I'd been looking at for four nights and couldn't sign for. I read it twice and signed it at twenty past two, and this time the nib went in like a nail into soft wood.

My fingers went first. They thickened round the pen till the knuckles disappeared, and when I tried to put it down I had to open my hand from the wrist, like a gate. By the time I'd switched the lamp off I couldn't make a fist. It didn't hurt the way the cough had. It just wouldn't let me close anything.
"Well," I told Dusty. "That one's mine, then."
He was already asleep.
Gil Ferrabee woke me at half eleven by leaning on the B1 bell. It took me three goes to do up my boots.
"They've stuck something on the door," he said. "A man with a staple gun. On the actual door."

The front door is the original: oak, a brass letter plate and about a century of paint. At head height somebody had stapled a laminated sheet into the wood. GREYFOLD PROPERTY PARTNERS, it said across the top, and underneath, in smaller capitals, NOTICE OF WRECKING PERMIT, and underneath that, that Pellory Court would be condemned and demolished if any of its public floors failed a structural inspection. HOLDER OF RECORD: I. TARRANT.
I read it twice, lips moving, with Gil breathing on my shoulder. I read the name at the top twice as well.
"Are they knocking us down?" Gil said.
"Only if the building fails an inspection," I said. "It won't. The stairs are sound. I'm up and down them every night."
A woman came up the steps with two coffees in a cardboard tray, good coat, flat shoes, and smiled at the notice, at Gil and at me as if we were just what she'd hoped for.

"You're the caretaker," she said. "I'm Imogen. I'm the name on that, I'm afraid. I'd rather you heard it from a person than a staple gun." She held out the tray. "One's yours. I guessed white, no sugar."
It was right. I took it, and it took both hands, and she saw.
"What've you done to your hands?"
"Door," I said. True enough.

"Ouch. Okay. Two ways this goes, honestly." She said it to me and Gil at once, which is a knack. "Either your stairs are as sound as they look, the inspector signs, and I'm a bad memory by spring. Or they're not, and we talk properly about where everyone lives next. Either way, nobody gets surprised by me." She tilted her head. "Sorry, I haven't asked your name."
"Ravi," I said. "Ravi Anand."
She went still. Half a second, less. The coffee in her hand didn't move at all.
"Anand," she said. "Fennick Lofts?"

The front door's top hinge had dropped. You could see it in the gap at the head of the door, wider on the latch side than the hinge side, a wedge of daylight you could have slid a coin into, and there was a fresh rub on the frame where the door caught on its way shut. Three steel butts, painted over so often they looked like part of the wood. The top one would have a worn pin, or the screws would have pulled in the old holes, and with oak that heavy it was only going one way.
"Your top hinge has dropped," I said. "On this door. It wants new pins. Maybe longer screws."
Imogen looked at the hinge. Then she looked at me, and her voice went down instead of up.
"Okay," she said. "Small city." She took a card out of her coat and set it on the post table, by Dusty's nose. "Ring me if anything cracks, Ravi. I mean that kindly."
She went down the steps like someone on time for the next thing. Gil read the notice a third time.
"She seemed nice," he said.
I drank the coffee. I'd have liked to hold the cup properly.

At four an e-bike came up Wickline Street too fast and stopped at the kerb in a way that made me think about brake pads. The rider pulled off a helmet with a cartoon owl on it: nineteen at most, an Errandry bag on their back.

"Pellory Court," they said, to the phone and then to me. "Left off the high street, right at the launderette, under the scaffolding that isn't holding anything up, and you're here. Three stars. Your step's a trap. You the building?"
"I'm the caretaker."
"Close enough. Kit. Kit Dalisay." They swung the bag round and pulled out a parcel the size of a shoebox, brown paper and a lot of tape, with a printed label. "Got one for you. Well. Not for you."
OCCUPANT, 5-1, PELLORY COURT, the label said. LEAVE AT SERVICE-LIFT DOOR.

I read it twice. My fingers had set round the coffee cup that morning and stayed that shape, and I couldn't have taken the parcel off Kit if I'd wanted to. 5-1. The door on a floor nobody could see from the street, swollen in its frame, that I'd signed for at twenty past two and was carrying in every knuckle.
Kit was looking up at the front of the building, counting windows with one finger. One row, two, three, four. Then the roofline. Then back down at the phone.
"Which way's the fifth floor?" Kit said. "It says use the service lift."
